Oriental Institute Megiddo Expedition
Multi-period tell sequence; monumental gates; stables or storehouses; palace complexes; ivory cache; water system; Egyptian and Canaanite material.

Strong site identification and background: Megiddo was a strongly fortified royal city through many periods. Excavators found monumental fortifications and gates, palaces and water systems, including a 9th-century BC shaft and tunnel that BiblePlaces assigns to Ahab, and the site fits the Kings accounts of a key royal fortress.
claims.strength_reason: Three major digs (Schumacher, the University of Chicago, Yadin) uncovered twenty major occupation levels with monumental fortifications, gates, palaces and water systems (Megiddo Expedition, Past Excavations; BiblePlaces, Megiddo). What weakens it: the Expedition itself says nearly every layer and major building is the subject of fierce dispute, so the dating of individual structures is not part of this rating.

claims.text: Contested: did Solomon build Megiddo's gate, palaces and 'stables' (1 Kings 9:15)? One side: Yadin attributed Palace 6000 and the 'Solomonic' gate to Solomon, and Mazar & Bronk Ramsey (2008) date the start of Iron Age II (and the end of Megiddo VIA) to the first half of the 10th century BC, which allows a Solomonic date. Other side: Finkelstein & Piasetzky (2006) argue that radiocarbon supports the Low Chronology, which would move these buildings later, to the 9th-century Omride kings. No verdict.
claims.strength_reason: Side A, a 10th-century (Solomonic) date is possible: the Megiddo Expedition says Yadin dug Palace 6000, which is generally attributed to Solomon; BiblePlaces calls the gate 'Solomonic' after 1 Kings 9:15; Mazar & Bronk Ramsey's Bayesian models put the Iron I/II transition at Megiddo at about 967–943 BC. Side B, the Low Chronology: Finkelstein & Piasetzky's abstract says the full Tel Rehov dates support the Low Chronology and points to sample selection problems. What weakens both: each side says the other's radiocarbon models depend on which samples are used. The Expedition calls the stables 'so-called' and says the dates are fiercely disputed.

Tel Aviv University Lachish Expedition
Detailed siege-ramp excavation; Level III = Assyrian 701 BCE destruction; Level II = Babylonian 588/6 BCE; gate complex; Judean palace.

Strong evidence for the Assyrian assault (701 BC): Sennacherib's palace reliefs from Nineveh, now in the British Museum, show the siege of Lachish; the Assyrian siege ramp, with more than 1,000 iron arrowheads, was excavated at the site; and the current expedition dates the destruction of Level III to 701 BC. This matches 2 Kings 18:14 (Sennacherib at Lachish).
claims.strength_reason: Three separate lines of evidence agree: the British Museum's Lachish relief panels (BM 124911, South-West Palace, Nineveh, 700–692 BC) show Sennacherib receiving the capture of Lachish; BiblePlaces describes the excavated siege ramp with more than 1,000 arrowheads, which the reliefs depict; the BAS stratigraphy table puts the Level III destruction at 701 BC. What weakens it: the reliefs are royal propaganda with stylized scenes, and the Level III = 701 BC link is labeled 'as interpreted by the current expedition' (Ussishkin's Tel Aviv University dig; his 1990 Tel Aviv paper was read only as Crossref metadata).

claims.text: Good evidence for the Babylonian assault (588/586 BC): the current expedition assigns the final Judean city (Level II) and its destruction to the Babylonian conquest. The Lachish Letters, ink notes on potsherds, came from this level at the city gate. Letter 4 says the writer was watching for Lachish's signal fires because Azekah's could no longer be seen. This fits Jeremiah 34:7, where Lachish and Azekah are the last fortified cities of Judah left.
claims.strength_reason: Checkable finds: the BAS stratigraphy table lists Level II with 'the Lachish letters', ended by the Babylonian conquest in 588/6 BC; the British Museum's Lachish Letter II (BM 125702) gives its findspot as the gate bastion room E.18:C; BiblePlaces quotes Letter 4 on the signal fires of Lachish and Azekah and ties it to Jeremiah 34:7. What weakens it: the sources read are summaries, not the final excavation reports; no Babylonian text naming Lachish was read; and linking Letter 4 to the last days before the fall is an interpretation (BiblePlaces says 'possibly'). So this is good evidence for the destruction, but the letter's exact moment is not proven.

claims.text: Strong site identification: Tel Gezer is biblical Gezer. C. Clermont-Ganneau identified the tell in 1871, and two years later he found the first of many boundary stones inscribed with the city's name. 1 Kings 9:16 names Gezer as the city Pharaoh burned and gave to Solomon's wife.
claims.strength_reason: Checkable finds: inscribed boundary stones naming Gezer, found from 1873 on (BiblePlaces, Gezer). That is direct written evidence on the ground, not just name similarity. What weakens it: nothing serious for the identification. It does not by itself date any building to Solomon (see C04098b).

claims.text: Contested: is Gezer's monumental (six-chambered) gate Solomon's work (1 Kings 9:15-17)? One side: BiblePlaces, following the excavators (Dever), dates the gate to Solomon, like those at Hazor and Megiddo. It sits on a destruction layer linked to the Pharaoh of 1 Kings 9:16, with a later destruction tied to Shishak (about 925 BC). Other side: Finkelstein's Low Chronology moves these gates later, into the 9th century BC (Finkelstein 2002; Dever replied in 2003). No verdict.
claims.strength_reason: Side A, Solomonic: BiblePlaces dates the gate by the destruction level beneath it and a second destruction soon after (Shishak, about 925 BC). Mazar & Bronk Ramsey (2008, Radiocarbon) put the Iron I/II transition in the first half of the 10th century BC, which allows it. Side B, the Low Chronology: Finkelstein & Piasetzky (2006, Radiocarbon) argue that radiocarbon supports lower dates. Finkelstein 'Gezer Revisited and Revised' (Tel Aviv 2002) and Dever's 'Visiting the Real Gezer: A Reply' (Tel Aviv 2003) carry the Gezer-specific debate; both were read only as Crossref metadata. What weakens both: the dating hangs on pottery phases and radiocarbon models, and BiblePlaces itself notes that Macalister's early dig destroyed much of the stratigraphy.

A team led from the University of Haifa, with T. E. Levy, published a detailed study of a wood-and-lead anchor stock in the Dor (Tantura) Lagoon. Found in 1994–95 and first dated to the Persian period, it belongs to a cargo of amphorae and nine iron blooms. Radiocarbon dates from the anchor and the cargo place it in the late 7th to early 6th century BCE, making it one of the earliest composite wood-and-lead anchors in the Mediterranean. The stock is about 2.2 m long; its four lead cores are estimated at about 113 kg, for a total stock weight of about 150 kg.

Most scholars identify Tell ed-Damiyeh (Tall Dāmiyā), on the east bank near where the Zarqa joins the Jordan, with the town of Adam in Joshua 3:16. The Arabic name Damiya echoes Adam, and surveys found pottery from the Late Bronze and Iron Ages onward.
claims.strength_reason: Checkable: Watson (PEFQS 1895) places Tell Damieh on the east bank by the Wady Zerka with 'remains of an ancient town'; the Damiya catalog page quotes Petit & Kafafi (2016) that most scholars identify it with Adam(ah) and lists survey pottery from LB II, Iron I and Iron II. What weakens it: the case rests on name likeness plus location; Petit & Kafafi note that the tell is small (about 3 ha), and they fold in 'Admah' of Genesis 14, which is a different name. In Joshua 3:16 the KJV (Qere) says the water heaped up 'very far from the city Adam', while the RV (Kethib) says 'at Adam' (Dalton 1895), so Adam is a reference point either way, not necessarily the spot of the heap.

claims.text: In December 1267 the Jordan reportedly stopped flowing near Damiya. A high bank (a 'mound overlooking the river') fell in and dammed it from about midnight until mid-morning, so Sultan Baybars' builders repaired the piers of his new bridge in the dry riverbed. The account comes from the 14th-century Arab historian al-Nuwayri.
claims.strength_reason: Checkable: Watson (PEFQS 1895, free PDF) gives Clermont-Ganneau's translation of al-Nuwayri: the bridge 'in the neighbourhood of Damieh', the water stopping 'in the night preceding the dawn' of 17 Rabi I 666 AH (8 Dec 1267), riders finding a fallen mound damming the river, and the flow returning 'at the fourth hour of the day'. What weakens it: it is one chronicle written decades later; Watson relays Clermont-Ganneau's readings of obscure manuscript words; the bridge order is dated 664 AH (1266) and the stoppage 666 AH (1267), so packs cite both years; the exact spot of the collapse upstream is not fixed. It shows a natural damming can happen here, not how or when Joshua 3 happened.

The catalog does not quote the 1927 eyewitness reports; Garstang (1931) and the Avni studies were not read; other summaries give about 21 hours; and no source read pins the 1927 collapse to Damiya itself (one macroseismic study put the epicentre near the Damiya bridge, but it was seen only in a search abstract). A simple copper-alloy sealing ring found at Herodium in Gideon Foerster's 1968–69 dig, and published in 2018, has a krater (wine bowl) engraved on it with tiny Greek letters read as 'of Pilatus'. The publishing team said it was unlikely to be Pontius Pilate's own ring, but raised the possibility that it belonged to someone in his administration or to another man named Pilatus.
claims.strength_reason: Checkable find: the ring, its findspot (Herodium, in a layer buried before the fortress fell in 71 CE) and the reading Πιλάτο(υ) are reported in the 2018 IEJ article (JSTOR 26740648). Eck & Ecker's 2024 abstract, which was read, confirms the 1968/69 Foerster find, the 2018 publication and the reading 'of Pilate', and says the published interpretations all linked the ring 'directly or indirectly' to Pilate. What weakens this side: the 2018 authors themselves call a link to Pontius Pilate only a possibility. Pilatus was a family name used by others, the letters are small and partly deformed, and the ring's krater is a Jewish motif made locally. The IEJ article was not opened directly (JSTOR access challenge).

claims.text: Werner Eck and Avner Ecker (ʿAtiqot 2024) argue the ring is not connected to Pontius Pilate. They say the reading itself is problematic. A Roman official's ring would use Latin, the language of Roman administration in the early 1st century, not Greek. And the ring more probably belonged to a local Jew. They also discuss other ways to read the letters.
claims.strength_reason: Checkable source: the ʿAtiqot 110 abstract (doi.org/10.70967/2948-040X.1083, read) states that 'apart from the problematic reading', everything known about Roman provincial administration, especially the use of Greek in an administrative context in the first half of the 1st century, speaks against linking the ring to Pilate, and that alternative readings are discussed. What weakens this side: it is an argument from Roman practice and epigraphy, not a new find; it does not prove whose ring it was. The full PDF could not be fetched (403), so only the abstract was read.

claims.text: Korazim Synagogue and Town Excavations
Basalt synagogue (mainly 3rd–4th c.
CE) with ornate benches and ‘Seat of Moses’; town remains; mikveh; olive presses—Galilean Jewish village of Roman–Byzantine periods.

Place-name continuity: the ruins called Khirbet Karazeh (Korazim) keep a form of the name Chorazin, one of the towns Jesus denounced (Matthew 11:21; Luke 10:13). Eusebius (early 4th century) describes Chorazin as a deserted village two miles from Capernaum, which fits the location of these ruins.
claims.strength_reason: Checkable basis: BiblePlaces lists Kh. Karraza / Karazeh / Kerazeh / Korazim among the site's names. Eusebius' Onomasticon, entry 976 (Wolf 1971 translation on tertullian.org, read 2026-10-27), places Chorazin, the Galilee town Jesus reproached in the Gospel, as a deserted village two miles from Capernaum. The app's own pins put the ruins about 3.6 km from Capernaum in a straight line (2 Roman miles is about 3 km). Two independent lines, the surviving name and a 4th-century location, point to the same ruins, which is why it is rated strong. What weakens it: no inscription naming the town was read, and the visible synagogue is late Roman (BiblePlaces dates it to the 2nd century AD), not from Jesus' time. BiblePlaces also notes an unpublished 1926 report by J. Ory of an earlier building about 200 m west, which was not verified.

claims.text: Visible synagogue is later than Jesus; earlier settlement evidence exists but the famous carved synagogue is post-NT.
claims.strength_reason: The visible synagogue is a 'Galilean'-style basalt building (BiblePlaces, Chorazin), a type generally dated after the New Testament period, so it is not the synagogue of Jesus' day.

claims.text: Robinson's Arch fell after the Roman destruction of Jerusalem in 70 CE, according to the IAA excavators. Fallen Herodian stones still lie on the street below the wall. claims.strength_reason: The IAA's 2011 Robinson's Arch report (Shukron & Reich) states that the arch collapsed after the destruction of Jerusalem in 70 CE, and it shows that two fallen voussoirs in the drainage channel are NOT from that collapse (they fell during building). cosmic_airburst
A Middle Bronze Age destruction/abandonment horizon exists at TeH with ash, collapsed architecture, and unusual heat-affected pottery/mudbrick reported by excavators.
Proponents argued these matched a Tunguska-scale airburst ~1650 BCE.
Scientific Reports published that claim in 2021.
DOES NOT establish a confirmed cosmic airburst.
Jaret & Harris (2022) argued mineralogic/geochemical data fail impact-diagnostic criteria (shocked quartz not convincingly demonstrated; high-temp melts/geochemistry not uniquely extraterrestrial).
Boslough & Bruno (2025) showed Tunguska comparisons overestimated blast temperature/wind and cannot produce claimed melting at stated distances.
Image-manipulation concerns were raised (Bik / Retraction Watch).
Scientific Reports RETRACTED the Bunch et al. paper on 24 Apr 2025 (doi:10.1038/s41598-025-99265-5).
Authors largely disagreed and later republished expanded versions elsewhere (e.g.
Airbursts and Cratering Impacts / ScienceOpen).
Mainstream archaeology does not accept the airburst conclusion.

Gilgal, Israel's first camp after crossing the Jordan, lay east of Jericho toward the river. Its exact site is unknown. Josephus puts the camp about 10 furlongs (about 2 km) from Jericho and 50 furlongs from the Jordan; Eusebius places Galgala east of old Jericho, going toward the Jordan.
claims.strength_reason: Checkable: Joshua 4:19 ('in the east border of Jericho'); Josephus Ant. 5.20 (Perseus: 'ten furlongs from Jericho'); Eusebius' Onomasticon 311 (east of old Jericho toward the Jordan); Naʾaman (Tel Aviv 2024 abstract) treats biblical Gilgal as a single cult site east of Jericho. What weakens it: all of these are texts. No excavated remains from Joshua's time have been tied to any spot, and the ancient distances are approximate and measured from different Jerichos.

claims.text: Candidate: the Khirbet el-Mafjar area (Hisham's Palace), about 2 km northeast of Tell es-Sultan, fits Josephus' '10 furlongs from Jericho'. It has been proposed as Gilgal, and Schneider (1931) placed Byzantine Galgala there.
claims.strength_reason: Checkable: the OSM points for Tell es-Sultan and Qasr Hisham are 2.04 km apart, close to Josephus' 10 furlongs (about 1.9 km); the CMHL Galgala entry notes that Schneider identified the remains with Khirbet el-Mafjar. What weakens it: Muilenburg's 1955 BASOR case for this area (reported Iron Age sherds nearby) was read only as metadata; no Late Bronze or Iron Age camp remains were described in any source read; the visible ruins are the later Umayyad palace; and the distance fit depends on measuring from Tell es-Sultan.

claims.text: Khirbet en-Nitla, about 3 km east of Byzantine Jericho, is the Byzantine pilgrims' 'Galgala'. A church with five building phases (4th/5th–9th centuries) was excavated there. Pilgrims from 333 to about 700 CE describe twelve stones shown there, and the Madaba Map labels it 'Galgala, also the Twelve Stones'.
claims.strength_reason: Checkable: the CMHL church record 12921 lists the Kelso & Baramki excavation (five phases from a 4th–5th century basilica to a 9th-century chapel; coins of the 4th–8th centuries), the pilgrim texts (Bordeaux 333, Jerome 385/6, Theodosius c. 518–530, Piacenza c. 570, Adomnán c. 680s) and the Madaba Map label; Eusebius says the stones were shown about two miles from Jericho. What weakens it: the CMHL calls the excavators' stratigraphy problematic (finds not tied to loci); farming has since destroyed the site; and other scholars proposed Tell el-Matleb, Tell el-Jurn or el-Mafjar for Byzantine Galgala.

claims.text: As the Gilgal of Joshua's day, Khirbet en-Nitla is weak. Nothing from the Late Bronze or Iron Age is reported there; the identification comes from Byzantine pilgrim tradition more than 1,500 years later.
claims.strength_reason: Checkable: the CMHL record lists the pottery as Hellenistic to Byzantine and Early Islamic, and the coins as 4th–8th century CE, with no earlier remains. The site's identity rests on the 4th–7th century pilgrim texts and the Madaba Map. What weakens even this negative: the site is now destroyed and the old excavation was limited, so absence of earlier finds is not proof that nothing was there; Kelso & Baramki's report itself was read only as metadata.

claims.text: Card A — Zertal: Adam Zertal (University of Haifa) identified five large 'foot-shaped' stone enclosures in the Jordan Valley and nearby hills, among them Bedhat esh-Sha'ab and Yafit 3, as Israelite 'gilgal' assembly and ritual sites founded at the start of Iron Age I (13th–12th centuries BC).
claims.strength_reason: Checkable: the 2009 University of Haifa release (EurekAlert!) reports five enclosures found during the Manasseh Hill-Country Survey (1990–2008), two excavated in 2002–2005 under Ben-Yosef. Pottery and bones date their foundation to the end of the 13th century BC, and paved circuits are read as procession paths. Bar & Ben-Yosef (JSRS 2021 abstract) keep the Iron I founding and address the questions later raised about it. What weakens this side: the 'gilgal' and cultic reading is an interpretation of shape and setting; the release is a press statement; and these enclosures are not near Jericho, so they are not candidates for Joshua's single camp.

claims.text: Card B — critics: Nadav Naʾaman (Tel Aviv, 2024) argues that every biblical Gilgal is one cult site east of Jericho and that 'gilgals' as a type of site should be dropped. New ceramic and OSL dating at Bedhat esh-Sha'ab (Bar, Jacobi & Shamir 2023) puts its round unit in later Iron I–IIA and the central courtyard's main use in the Early Roman period, a more complex history than first proposed.
claims.strength_reason: Checkable: Naʾaman's abstract (TAU portal) says gilgal never appears in the Bible as a noun for a kind of settlement and that the plural 'gilgals' used by archaeologists is misleading. The 2023 JSRS abstract (U. Haifa portal) reports that unit U10 was built between late Iron I and Iron IIA and used into Iron IIB, while the main habitation of the central courtyard was Early Roman, 'contra earlier suggestions'. What weakens this side: Naʾaman's case is textual, not a dig; the 2023 dating covers one site and revises its dates without ruling out an Iron Age gathering use. Only the abstracts were read.
